'''Walter Bruno Gratzer''' (20 September 1932 – 20 October 2021) was a German-born British [[biophysical chemist]] and science writer.<ref name="The Guardian"/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Hargittai, Istvan|year=2022|title=Walter B. Gratzer (1932–2021) – molecular scientist and science writer|journal= Structural Chemistry|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11224-022-01942-y|volume=33|issue=3|pages=991–992|doi=10.1007/s11224-022-01942-y|bibcode=2022StrCh..33..991H }}</ref>

==Career==

Gratzer was born in a Jewish hospital in [[Breslau]] (now Wrocław).<ref>{{cite journal|year=2022|title=Walter Bruno Gratzer (1932–2021): In his own words, as far as possible|journal=Current Biology|url=https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(22)00567-X|volume=32|issue=9|pages=402–R404|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2022.04.002 |last1=Robertson |first1=Miranda |bibcode=2022CBio...32.R402R |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Gratzer and his parents escaped Nazi persecution by escaping to [[Czechoslovakia]] and the United Kingdom in 1939.<ref name="The Guardian">{{cite web |author=Ferry, Georgina| title=Walter Gratzer obituary |date=10 November 2021 |website=[[The Guardian]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230606025958/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/nov/10/walter-gratzer-obituary |archive-date=6 June 2023 |url-status=live |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/nov/10/walter-gratzer-obituary}}</ref> He lived in [[Belsize Park]] and then [[Cheltenham]]. He won a scholarship to [[Cheltenham grammar school]].<ref name="The Guardian"/>

Gratzer completed at [[University of Oxford]] a BA in chemistry in 1954, followed by an MA in 1958. His PhD was completed at [[National Institute for Medical Research]] in 1960. He was a research fellow at [[Harvard University]] from 1960 to 1963, a lecturer in biophysics at King's from 1963 to 1966, and worked at the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|Medical Research Council]] from 1966 to 1996.<ref>[http://www.kcl.ac.uk/schools/biohealth/research/randall/res-sections/biophysics/sleep/wgratzer "Professor Walter Gratzer"], [[King's College London]], accessed 7 November 2010. [https://web.archive.org/web/20101019135823/http://www.kcl.ac.uk/schools/biohealth/research/randall/res-sections/biophysics/sleep/wgratzer Archived] by [[WebCite]] on 7 November 2010.</ref>

He was professor of biophysical chemistry at [[King's College London]]<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Gratzer | first1 = W. | doi = 10.1186/1741-7007-9-12 | title = Biophysics - whence, whither, wherefore - or Hold that hyphen | journal = BMC Biology | volume = 9 | article-number = 12 | year = 2011 | pmid =  21371341| pmc =3055213 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and an author and reviewer of popular science. He was the first ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' news correspondent appointed by editor [[John Maddox]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Gratzer | first1 = W. | title = Obituary: John Maddox (1925–2009) | doi = 10.1038/458983a | journal = Nature | volume = 458 | issue = 7241 | pages = 983–984 | year = 2009 | pmid =  19396135| doi-access =  }}.</ref> Oliver Sacks of ''Nature'' writes that his reviews have high literary quality and show knowledge of a wide range of topics.<ref name=Sacks>{{cite journal | last1 = Sacks | first1 = Oliver | year = 2002| title = Bringing scientists to life | url = https://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v419/n6909/full/419786a.html | journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume = 419 | issue = 6909| page = 786 | doi = 10.1038/419786a | url-access = subscription }}</ref> Gratzer was a friend of [[James D. Watson]], and wrote the introduction and afterword of his ''A Passion for DNA''.<ref>Friedberg, Errol C. (2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=WR1GcZAR6RQC&pg=PA111 ''The Writing Life of James D. Watson''], [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press]], p.&nbsp;111. {{ISBN|0-87969-700-8}}.</ref> He died in London on 20 October 2021.<ref name="The Guardian"/>
